# Ignatious Presearch Memo: Figma, Inc.

## One-Page Brief

**Who and what:** Figma is the dominant browser-based, collaborative design and product-development platform (NYSE: FIG), founded 2012, IPO'd July 31, 2025 at $33/share. It priced at a ~$19.3B valuation, traded up to a ~$56.3B peak within days, and has since fallen roughly 75-85% from that peak to a market cap near $13-15B as of mid-August 2026, even as revenue keeps accelerating (48% YoY in Q2 2026).

**Posture call:** This is a first call, and per the banker the objective is to gauge whether Dylan Field is willing to sell. Do not treat this as a live sell-side mandate discussion. Dylan Field personally controls a majority of Figma's voting power through Class B super-voting stock and has said publicly and recently that he is glad to be independent. His own incentive structure (a ten-year CEO award with vesting tranches up to a $130 share price) is built for him to keep running Figma, not to sell it. Treat this as **first meeting, mixed counterparty posture**: the company (market, activist investor, some board dynamics) shows signs of pressure, but the one person who actually decides is not currently under personal or financial pressure to transact. The right posture is to earn credibility and diagnose real appetite indirectly, not to pitch a sale process.

**The play:**
1. Lead with a sharp, credible point of view on where design/AI-native software is heading, not with valuation or a sale pitch.
2. Use the banker's personal relationship with Dylan to open naturally; do not over-reference it or make the call feel transactional from minute one.
3. Probe gently on the things that are actually live and uncomfortable for Figma right now (the Findell Capital activist campaign, the Anthropic/Claude Design conflict, leadership churn) as market-informed observations, not gotchas.
4. Do not use the words "sale process," "acquirer," or "exit" unless Dylan raises them first. If he does, follow, don't lead.
5. Leave the door open for a second conversation; the success metric for this call is relationship and information, not a mandate.

## Company Context

### Funding, Cap Table, and Financial Position

Figma raised roughly $749M in venture funding across 7 rounds before its IPO, backed by Index Ventures (lead, seed), Greylock Partners, Kleiner Perkins, and Sequoia Capital as its largest institutional holders. It IPO'd on the NYSE on July 31, 2025 at $33/share (~$19.3B valuation), spiked to a peak market cap of roughly $56.3B in the first days of trading, and has since fallen to roughly $13.5-14.9B (as of August 2026), an approximately 75-85% decline from peak, even as the underlying business has kept accelerating: Q2 2026 revenue was $370.1M, up 48% year-over-year, its third straight quarter of accelerating growth, with net dollar retention of 136% and full-year 2026 guidance raised to $1.463-1.467B. The company ended Q2 2026 with $1.7B in cash and marketable securities and is not yet consistently profitable on a GAAP basis (Q2 2026 GAAP net loss was $112.2M, driven substantially by stock-based compensation). Figma is a controlled company: Dylan Field holds a majority of voting power via Class B common stock, and insiders overall hold roughly 45% of the company. Figma's insiders, including Field, have been active net sellers over the past year (approximately $96-111M net sold across insiders in relevant 12-month windows per multiple filings-based trackers), which is consistent with continued personal liquidity-taking rather than distress.

### SWOT (our takeaways, with a point of view)

| Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|
| Category-defining, high-switching-cost incumbent in collaborative product design; ~two-thirds of MAUs are non-designers, evidence the product has become general-purpose workflow infrastructure, not a niche design tool. | Governance overhang: unresolved conflict-of-interest questions around former director Mike Krieger's move to Anthropic and the immediately-following Claude Design launch, now the subject of activist demands for an independent investigation. |
| Accelerating growth (48% YoY in Q2 2026, third straight quarter of acceleration) with a raised full-year guide, at a scale (~$1.46B run rate) most "AI loser" narratives do not fit. | Elevated stock-based compensation (~27% of 2026 revenue per Findell's estimate, versus ~8% at Adobe), a real dilution and governance concern that an activist has now made public and specific. |
| $1.7B cash, no near-term financing need, and a demonstrated willingness to use the balance sheet for tuck-in AI acquisitions (Weavy/Figma Weave, Payload CMS, Bud). | Leadership churn concentrated in one earnings call: CPO departing, CMO departing, CTO moving to a new "chief architect" role with a CTO search underway, all announced August 5, 2026, a level of simultaneous transition that invites scrutiny of execution risk. |
| Deep technical integration across the AI ecosystem (OpenAI, Anthropic (historically), Google, GitHub, Microsoft dev tools) gives it leverage as an AI-agnostic layer rather than a single-model bet. | Founder-controlled structure means no external party, including the board or activists, can force a transaction; this cuts both ways as a strength for stability but a wall against any process we might otherwise help engineer. |

| Opportunities | Threats |
|---|---|
| Activist pressure (Findell) is already pushing the board toward "maximize shareholder value" language publicly, which can make the environment more receptive to strategic dialogue over time even without Dylan actively shopping the company. | Direct new entrant competition from frontier AI labs themselves (Anthropic's Claude Design), which changes Figma's competitive set from other design tools to the model providers it depends on for AI features. |
| "Code on the Canvas" and Figma Make position Figma to own a wider swath of the software creation pipeline as AI collapses the design-to-code boundary, expanding its addressable market and its strategic value to a buyer far beyond "a design tool." | Continued AI-driven commoditization narrative risk: even strong quarters have not durably re-rated the stock, suggesting the market may keep discounting Figma regardless of fundamentals until a structural resolution (M&A, buyback, or multi-quarter margin proof) changes the story. |
| Public market discount (trading well below the $20B Adobe once agreed to pay, at 3x the revenue) creates an unusually attractive entry point for a strategic buyer relative to 2022 economics, if Dylan's calculus ever shifts. | Regulatory precedent: the same UK/EU competition concerns that killed the Adobe deal in 2023 have not gone away, and would resurface hard against Adobe or possibly Canva as an acquirer, structurally narrowing the credible buyer list for a full-scale strategic combination. |
